claims.text: Slow cooling after vacuum sintering of additively manufactured refractory HEAs produces a multiphase microstructure.
Conventionally slow-cooled, vacuum-sintered HEA components have significant residual stresses.
The baseline multiphase microstructure and residual stresses compromise dimensional fidelity and mechanical integrity.
Rapid water quenching should replace conventional slow cooling immediately after vacuum sintering.
Refractory HEA components can be made by 3D ink-extrusion printing followed by vacuum sintering.
The proposed treatment is intended for refractory HEAs processed under sintering conditions similar to those used for ink-printed equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Rapid quenching limits atomic diffusion during cooling.
Limiting diffusion during cooling prevents extensive phase separation.
Rapid quenching prevents grain growth and produces a refined grain structure.
Rapid quenching yields a metastable single-phase microstructure.
The quenched microstructure has lower residual stress and fewer internal defects than the slow-cooled microstructure.
A more uniform microstructure with lower residual stress improves dimensional precision.
A more uniform microstructure with lower residual stress improves mechanical integrity.
Relative to slow cooling, water-quenched components will have smaller dimensional deviations.
Relative to slow cooling, water-quenched components will have higher hardness and yield strength.
Relative to slow cooling, water-quenched components will have lower defect density.
The expected effect may change with alloy composition, component geometry, or sintering parameters.

Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, residual stress, and mechanical properties relative to an otherwise identical slow-cooled control would falsify the hypothesis.
